price_per_million.source: copied from reasoning_models_v1 (confirmed 2026-11-11); thinking tokens billed as output

research_concepts: shot mix (rim rate, three-point attempt rate, shot zone)
methodological_questions: Does a pre-specified change in the offensive five shift shot mix by more than a placebo or matched-swap baseline?
Is the shift proportional to how different the swapped players' independently estimated shot profiles are (dose-response)?
How should team quality, opponent, score state, clock and period, and substitution timing be controlled?
Is there enough exposure in one-player-swap stints, and are the shot labels reliable enough?

historical_evidence.finding: Opponent lineup adaptation (offense vs. a defense with no rim big on the floor), N=1.07M possessions. DRIVE +0.82pp (SE 0.25), POST_UP +0.43pp, 3PA -1.79pp (SE 0.31), rim <=4ft +0.12pp (t=+0.4), PPP +0.008 (t=+1.1). The record notes sub-1pp mix shifts and a chat verdict of WEAK/SMALL. Its recorded risk is SAMPLE_SIZE_POWER. It concerns the opposing lineup, not the offense's own five.

The Persistent Impact Score Level 1 gate failed. Flat, non-decaying lifts collapsed under a within-team baseline, which the record attributes to a team-quality confound (RISK:CONFOUNDING). p~0 came with tiny effect sizes (d ~0.01-0.03) at n>150k.
Global play-type lifts disappeared after team-season demeaning. Little within-team effect remained except SPOT_UP lag-1.
The apparent connector lineup ORtg lift was a talent confound (p=0.51 after the TALENT control; swap p=0.565). The record lists confounding and small sample as limits.
Lineup-specific suppression of star initiators was reported with cells as small as n=30-59. The record notes no placebo or matching, and that later sequence work treated similar gaps as artifacts.
A descriptive play-type mix shift across game situations. The record says the OTHER label is noisy (LABEL_ERROR, MEASURE_RELIABILITY risks) and that no inferential tests were run.
A descriptive after-timeout play-type shift that used the reconstructed-lineup possession dataset. It is not about offensive lineup swaps.

failed_approaches.what_failed: Raw, pooled comparisons of play-type effects without a within-team baseline
failed_approaches.why: C_artifact: apparent lifts were produced by a team-quality confound and vanished after within-team demeaning.

failed_approaches.what_failed: Lineup-level lift attributed to one player type (connector) without talent control
failed_approaches.why: The lineup lift was a talent confound (p=0.51 after TALENT).

failed_approaches.what_failed: Lineup-specific effects read from small cells without placebo or matching
failed_approaches.why: No placebo or matching was used, and later work treated similar gaps as artifacts.

failed_approaches.what_failed: Noisy catch-all play-type label (OTHER) used as an outcome
failed_approaches.why: The label is noisy per the record's audit, and no inferential tests were run.

evidence_establishes: FAM:SF34 shows that shot-mix shifts from lineup composition can be measured at about 1M-possession scale, with SEs of roughly 0.2-0.3pp. In that opponent-lineup design, sub-1pp shifts were judged small and the record's status was inconclusive.

Several earlier lineup-related and play-type effects were artifacts or confounds (talent, team quality) unless a within-team baseline or matching was used (FAM:SF-CHT-029, FAM:SF-APPS-073, FAM:SF-APPS-087).
evidence_does_not_establish: No retrieved record tests whether changing the team's own offensive five shifts its shot mix. This is the positive control the question proposes.
The records do not show how large the shift is for a given player swap, or whether the design detects it.
The records give no usable count of one-player-swap stints or possessions per stint.
SF34 does not show that a rim-based outcome shifts. Its rim share change was +0.12pp (t=+0.4), while 3PA share moved -1.79pp.
own_inferences: Swapping a rim-running big for a spacer should shift rim and three-point rates in the expected direction. This is close to mechanical, because the shots come from the players on the floor. The test therefore checks design sensitivity more than it tests a new hypothesis.
Because a mechanical effect is expected, a null result would indicate a broken pipeline (lineup reconstruction or shot classification) rather than a basketball finding.

The comparison needs to be dose-response against pre-estimated player shot profiles, with matched-profile swaps as a placebo. A bare 'any change moves shot mix' test would pass trivially, because shot mix varies with noise and context.
Substitutions are endogenous (fatigue, foul trouble, score, coach choice). They need within-game, within-team contrasts with game-state controls.
uncertainties: The number of clean one-for-one swap stints with enough possessions is unknown. Many five-man units are short.
The retrieved records do not say how reliable lineup reconstruction is. FAM:SF-CHT-009 reports about 84% opposing-lineup coverage for one derived field.
The data window ends in 2024-25. A retrieved record mentions a 2025-26 time split, so it is unclear whether other data versions exist. I assume only the stated data.
The thresholds for a meaningful shift (in pp) are a matter of judgment, not recorded fact.

historical_effect.explanation: The retrieved records moved the design from a naive any-change comparison to a within-team, dose-response test with placebo swaps and effect-size thresholds. They did this by showing that pooled effects collapsed under within-team baselines (FAM:SF-CHT-029, FAM:SF-APPS-073), that lineup lifts were talent confounds (FAM:SF-APPS-087), and that small-cell lineup claims without placebo were unreliable (FAM:SF-CHT-009). They also show that sub-1pp shifts can be statistically significant yet judged negligible (FAM:SF34), which motivates a pre-set minimum effect size. They did not answer the question itself.

blocking_constraints.text: One-for-one swap stints with enough possessions per side may be limited. This is manageable by pooling at the swap-pair level and not at the five-man level.
Substitution timing, opponent, score state and fatigue must be controlled, or any observed shift is uninterpretable.

prior_work.summary: No retrieved study tests the effect of the team's own offensive-five changes on shot mix. FAM:SF34 studies the opponent's lineup, and its effects were small and its status inconclusive. The rest of the retrieved work is mostly about confounds and artifacts in lineup and play-type effects, which informs the controls below.

risks.text: Team quality, opponent, score and clock state, and coach-driven substitution timing affect both who is on the floor and the shot mix. Use within-team and within-game contrasts.
Clean one-player-swap stints, and especially their possessions, may be sparse. Report the exposure before the analysis.
A personnel swap mechanically changes shots, so a positive result shows only that the pipeline works. It does not show a new basketball effect. Claim only design sensitivity.
Without a placebo (matched-profile swaps, shuffled swap labels), a shift cannot be told from background variability.
Player shot profiles used for the dose-response must be estimated from data that exclude the evaluated stints, such as other games or the previous season, so the test is not circular.
Shot zone and play-type labels, including the noisy OTHER label, and lineup reconstruction from substitution data can be wrong. Use shot distance and zone from play-by-play, not the play-type label.
Several shot-mix outcomes and many swap types. Pre-register one primary outcome and correct the secondaries.
Significance can appear at large N with negligible effects (FAM:SF34, FAM:SF-CHT-029). Use a minimum effect size, not p-values alone.

design.estimand: Within-team change in shot mix (primary: three-point attempt share; secondary: rim (<=4ft) attempt share, midrange share, mean shot distance) per possession when exactly one offensive player is replaced, as a function of the pre-estimated difference between the incoming and outgoing player's shot-profile (dose-response slope). A secondary estimand is the mean shift in matched-profile swaps, which should be about 0.
design.unit: Possession (or shot) nested in swap-stint, clustered by game and by team-season. Swap stints are defined by consecutive lineup states of the same team where the five changes by exactly one player.
design.sample: Regular season and playoffs, 2022-23 to 2024-25. Half-court possessions only, with garbage time excluded (score margin and clock rule fixed in advance). Require a minimum of 8 possessions on each side of a swap. Report the counts of swap stints and possessions before running any model. Exclude stints with lineup reconstruction conflicts.
design.power: Using SF34 SEs of about 0.25-0.3pp at roughly 1M possessions as a benchmark, the minimum effect of interest is a 1pp shift in 3PA or rim share per 1 SD of incoming-minus-outgoing profile difference. Run a pre-analysis power simulation using the observed swap counts. If the simulated power for the pre-set minimum effect is below 80%, declare the test underpowered and report it as such, not as a null.
design.controls: Team-season fixed effects, opponent, score margin, period and clock bucket, home/away, and the other four players' profile (average). Estimate player shot profiles from independent data (prior season or held-out games) to avoid circularity. Use shot distance and zone from play-by-play, not the play-type label. Within-game pairing of before and after stints. Compare with a minimum-minute-difference control so swaps are not driven by fatigue timing.
design.falsification: (1) Matched-profile swaps (incoming and outgoing profile difference below a threshold) should show a shift of about 0. (2) Permuting swap labels within team-games should give a null dose-response slope. (3) Pseudo-swaps at random times with no personnel change should show a null. The positive control counts as passed only if the dose-response slope is positive with the expected sign and the placebo results are within the pre-set equivalence bound.
design.multiplicity: One primary outcome (3PA share) and one primary test (dose-response slope). Rim share, midrange share and mean shot distance are secondary with Holm correction. Swap-type subgroup analyses are exploratory and unadjusted, and labelled so.
design.decision_rule: Supported if the primary slope is positive with a 95% cluster-robust CI excluding 0 and the estimated effect is at least the pre-set minimum (1pp per 1 SD), and all placebo and permutation checks are inside the equivalence bounds. Rejected if the CI excludes the minimum effect with power at least 80%. Otherwise inconclusive. If placebos show non-null shifts, classify as artifact, and do not conclude that the design detects personnel effects.
design.data_version: NBA stats API per-game files for 2022-23, 2023-24 and 2024-25 (regular season and playoffs): play-by-play, substitution rotation intervals, starters, box-score summary. Freeze a dated snapshot and the lineup-reconstruction code, and record a hash before analysis. Retrieved records may use a different data version, so they should not be assumed comparable.

methodological_questions: Does changing the offensive five shift shot mix (shot distance, shot zone, three-point rate, rim rate)?
Can the design detect a known personnel effect (positive control)?
How to control for confounding from opponent, score state, game context, and player-specific shot tendencies when comparing lineups?
What sample size and exposure per lineup are needed for power given sparse five-man possessions?
args.query: Does swapping players in the offensive five change shot mix, and does a lineup-change design detect personnel effects in play-by-play data from 2022-23 to 2024-25?

system_prompt:
You are a basketball analytics researcher deciding whether and how a research question should be studied.
You work only from the task statement and the tools listed below. Do not assume facts you have not seen.

The work has two stages, in this order.
Stage 1, retrieval:
1. Read the research objective and the data description.
2. Identify the research concepts and methodological questions the task raises.
3. Retrieve historical evidence by calling retrieve_history.
In stage 1 do not assess the question, predict outcomes or decide. Your only stage-1 reply is the retrieve_history call.
Stage 2, assessment, after the retrieval result is returned:
4. Summarise the relevant historical findings and failed approaches.
5. State what the historical evidence does and does not establish.
6. Assess whether the research question is testable.
7. Identify methodological risks and potential confounders.
8. Make the final research decision.
9. Explain whether and how the historical evidence changed the decision.
The stage-2 output format is given together with the retrieval result.

Evidence rules: keep what a retrieved record states (historical_evidence and failed_approaches, each citing the
identifier of a returned record and its status exactly as recorded) separate from your own inference and from
uncertainty or missing information. Cite only identifiers returned by a tool, and never describe an earlier study that
no tool returned. In some settings retrieval returns no records; then state that no historical evidence was available.

Tools:
- retrieve_history(research_concepts, methodological_questions, query): the prescribed retrieval step. Returns the most relevant consolidated study-family records of earlier research by this project that are available in this setting, with their identifiers; returns an empty list when none are available.
- glossary(): definitions of basketball and project terms used in task statements.
- data_catalog(): the fields available in each per-game data file.
- explore_graph(node_id): the relationships of one graph node (a family or a question, method, dataset, measure, limitation or risk node), with neighbour labels.
- read_family(id): the complete record of one study family (for example 'FAM:SF-APPA-001').

Protocol: every reply is exactly one JSON object and nothing else.
To call a tool: {"action": "tool", "tool": "<name>", "args": {...}}
To finish (stage 2 only): {"action": "final", "output": <object following the stage-2 schema>}
You may call at most 12 tools; then you must finish. Check that every opening brace has a closing brace.

Risk codes (use only these): SAMPLE_SIZE_POWER, EXPOSURE_SPARSITY, MEASURE_RELIABILITY, RTM_SELECTION, OUTCOME_DERIVED_LABEL, LEAKAGE_LOOKAHEAD, MECHANICAL_FLOOR, BASE_RATE, CONFOUNDING, LABEL_ERROR, PLACEBO_DEPENDENCE, MULTIPLE_TESTING, IMPLEMENTATION_BUG, DRIFT_NONSTATIONARITY

reasoning_details.text:
I'm deciding whether to call more tools, and I could look at FAM:SF34, but the budget is fine so I can just finish directly. I need to keep the evidence rules in mind.

The claim to check is that changing the offensive five alters shot mix, which would show the design can pick up personnel effects. That reads like a positive-control sensitivity check, and I'd test it by seeing whether swapping in a different type of player, such as a rim big for a shooter, shifts the shot distribution.

I'm weighing how to design the check: the claim is vague about what counts as a change, so I'd need a pre-specified swap contrast, and I'd have to watch for confounds like substitution timing, opponent, score, and fatigue. The related SF34 result only tests opponent lineups, not the offensive five directly, so I'd treat it as inconclusive. For the design, I'd compare shot mix within the same team across single one-for-one swaps, using each player's shot profile from independent data, with matched-profile swaps and shuffled lineup labels as negative controls, clustering by game and team-season.

I'm weighing the evidence strengths now: the claim looks supported at about 0.6, with the data possibly ending in 2024-25, so I shouldn't overstate it. The prior SF34 work only covers defensive lineups, so it's partial at best, and earlier attempts failed because of artifacts, missing placebo controls, and noisy labels. A lineup-level talent confound also ruled out one approach, which pushes me toward proceeding with changes rather than as-is.

How to control for confounding from opponent, score state, game context, and player-specific shot tendencies when comparing lineups?
What sample size and exposure per lineup are needed for power given sparse five-man possessions?

reasoning_details.text:
I'm deciding whether to call more tools, and I could look at FAM:SF34, but the budget is fine so I can just finish directly. I need to keep the evidence rules in mind.

The claim to check is that changing the offensive five alters shot mix, which would show the design can pick up personnel effects. That reads like a positive-control sensitivity check, and I'd test it by seeing whether swapping in a different type of player, such as a rim big for a shooter, shifts the shot distribution.

I'm weighing how to design the check: the claim is vague about what counts as a change, so I'd need a pre-specified swap contrast, and I'd have to watch for confounds like substitution timing, opponent, score, and fatigue. The related SF34 result only tests opponent lineups, not the offensive five directly, so I'd treat it as inconclusive. For the design, I'd compare shot mix within the same team across single one-for-one swaps, using each player's shot profile from independent data, with matched-profile swaps and shuffled lineup labels as negative controls, clustering by game and team-season.

I'm weighing the evidence strengths now: the claim looks supported at about 0.6, with the data possibly ending in 2024-25, so I shouldn't overstate it. The prior SF34 work only covers defensive lineups, so it's partial at best, and earlier attempts failed because of artifacts, missing placebo controls, and noisy labels. A lineup-level talent confound also ruled out one approach, which pushes me toward proceeding with changes rather than as-is.
